what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Cheating the meter is rare and costs nothing
sections.para: The reading meter lives in the browser, so anyone can edit the balance, open a private window or forge a £5 credit. Looking at kinds of reader rather than attackers, cheating is rare and costless. The real risks are a shared computer revealing history, confused readers and card fraud on the payment link.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Design for the readers who pay, not the cheaters
sections.para: Nine ways to cheat or leak are documented and accepted. Eight kinds of reader run from invisible engineers to people who can barely click, with agents moving between them. Cheating changes only a number the cheater sees, so the design serves the middle readers who will pay and avoids frightening those at the bottom.

sections.label: The question one level down
sections.line: Ask who will cheat, not who could
sections.para: Who are you protecting against ranked attackers; a meter that blocks nothing needs the question asked of non-malicious readers. Nobody breaks a meter to read a page already free to read. The question is whether they will, how many there are and the cost, given a depth charge, negative balances and an unverified £5 Stripe top-up.

sections.label: Eight kinds of reader
sections.line: Few readers could cheat; many could be confused
sections.para: Developers are about 0.6% of internet users, 36.5 million of 6.0 billion; Tor has about 3.1 to 3.3 million daily users. VPN users are about 23% and ad blockers 29%. In OECD tests 26% of adults could not use a computer, so confusion threatens far more readers than cheating.

sections.label: Agents change level in a single request
sections.line: Agents move between reader levels within one request
sections.para: An agent can read the unmetered markdown twin, drive a browser running the meter and reset storage between tasks. Agents are therefore outside the meter on purpose. Metering them properly would mean per-question pricing paid by the operator, and a browser meter would mostly charge honest agents.

sections.label: Nine ways to cheat or leak
sections.line: Six cheats cost nothing; three leaks are real
sections.para: Editing the balance, private windows, forged or replayed return URLs, clearing data and reading as an agent change only the cheater's own number, so they are accepted and the return page is deliberately unprotected. Shared-computer history, an injected script and Stripe card fraud are the leaks. Payment is the default everywhere.

sections.label: The risks that will actually happen
sections.line: Confusion, shared computers and card fraud are the risks
sections.para: Most likely is a vulnerable reader thinking a negative balance is debt, so the balance is small and explained and nothing blocks. A shared computer reveals history, cleared by Start again, and Stripe handles card testing on its link; cheating comes last, and an injected script needs a site hole first.

sections.label: Aim at the readers who will pay
sections.line: Building for the top would hurt the readers below
sections.para: Servers, accounts and sign-ins would stop no skilled cheater yet worsen the meter for readers who might pay or must not be frightened. So the payer gets one click, instruction followers see the gap published with its reason, struggling readers are never blocked or shamed, and experts may change their number.

sections.label: What would change the answer
sections.line: Unlocking content or syncing history would change the design
sections.para: If the balance unlocked anything, cheating would need a server or signed receipt. Synced history would sit in a reader-keyed encrypted vault, and cheating visible in Stripe would show it mattered. Sources include SlashData, the ITU, Tor metrics, GWI via DataReportal, Statista and the OECD survey via Nielsen Norman Group.
